newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia PM says Khmer Rouge leader in peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia PM says Khmer Rouge leader in peace talks.

text.p: Nominal Khmer Rouge leader Khieu Samphan has requested a meeting with Cambodian officials to forge an end to the rebels' long war with the government, the first prime minister said on Thursday.
Co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh said he had sent military officials on Thursday morning to meet Khieu Samphan at an undisclosed location.

"Mr Khieu Samphan requested us to meet this morning, so the (Cambodian officials) have already gone and this evening when they return, they will report to me," Ranariddh told reporters after a school graduation ceremony.
He would not reveal the location of meeting, only noting it would take place "with support from a country that is a friend of Cambodia".

Other top hard-liners, including hated leader Pol Pot -- mastermind of the 1975-1979 "killing fields" rule in which more than one million died -- powerful northwest commander Ta Mok and military chief Son Sen, were not participating in the negotiations, Ranariddh said.
He said Pol Pot may have already left the country but Thai military sources familiar with the issue disputed this.
The Bangkok Post on Thursday reported that Pol Pot, Ta Mok and Son Sen had left Cambodia by crossing the border into Thailand and were now in Bangkok.
"I cannot confirm or deny the report in the Bangkok Post, because I didn't read it. But he (Pol Pot) may have left already," Ranariddh said.
On Wednesday, Khieu Samphan revealed an apparent split within the top ranks of the Khmer Rouge when he accused Son Sen of spying for co-Premier Hun Sen.

Hun Sen said he had no knowledge of any spying within the Khmer Rouge, which has waged a low-intensity war against the coalition government since reneging on the 1991 U.N.-sponsored peace pact that led to the 1993 elections.
Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who formed an uneasy coalition after the elections, have been at odds over government policy toward the rebels and competed to recruit defectors to their own sides.
Since last August, thousands of guerrillas have defected to the government and fewer than 2,000 fighters are thought to remain in the last rebel stronghold of Anlong Veng in the country's north.
Ranariddh said that while he was "terribly sorry" that Hun Sen did not approve of the current negotiations, he nonetheless considered them to be talks on behalf of all Cambodians.
"The negotiations between Nhiek Bun Chhay and Khieu Samphan are negotiations between the government and the Khmer Rouge hard-liners, not just Ranariddh and (his) FUNCINPEC (party)," he said.
"If the result comes out positively, it will be a historic moment for all of Cambodia to have a peaceful end to the war," he said.
